transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, I, uh... I came in because things have been getting weird at night. I work as an animal caretaker, mostly with the big cats at the sanctuary, and they have this very strict feeding schedule, you know? Like, down to the ounce, at the exact same time every day. It's fascinating how routine-oriented they are. But for me... once I get home and I'm alone, if I start eating, it just... it feels like something completely takes over. I can't stop. Even while I'm literally standing there telling myself to put the food away, my hands just keep going. It's frustrating. The tigers, they eat their portion and they're done, they go to sleep. I wish I could just do that. But yeah, I just can't seem to stop myself once I start.
When you say you can't stop yourself once you start eating, does this happen even when you're not particularly hungry, and how do you feel afterward — do you feel guilt or shame?

Yeah, it's... it's exactly like that. I'm not even hungry a lot of the time. Especially on nights after late shifts, I just... I get home and it's like a switch flips. I'll eat a full frozen pizza, then just start eating cereal straight from the box, dig through whatever leftovers are in the fridge, grab whatever snacks are in the cabinet... all within an hour or two. It's way more than I'd ever eat in front of anyone. 

Actually, speaking of leftovers, my coworker brought in this amazing lasagna the other day. She makes it with this specific blend of cheeses she gets from a little Italian market downtown. It's incredible. We usually share lunch in the breakroom, which overlooks the lion enclosure. You should see them when they smell meat cooking in the microwave—they get so alert, pacing the fence line. It's kind of intimidating, honestly, just knowing how powerful they are. One time, this new volunteer dropped a bucket of chicken near the fence, and... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the eating. Yeah, I definitely feel guilty afterward. It's just awful.
Can you describe what it feels like just before and during these eating episodes? Do you feel like you’re not in control, even though you want to stop?

Yeah, like I was saying when I first sat down, it's exactly that. I'll literally be standing there in the kitchen, holding the food, screaming at myself in my head to just put it away, but my hands just keep going. It really does feel like something else takes over completely and I have zero control. It's almost like muscle memory just hijacks my brain. 

Which is weird to think about, because muscle memory is actually huge in my job. When you're prepping eighty pounds of raw meat in the morning, you kind of have to just zone out and let your hands do the work. We have this one older puma, Barnaby—he's a rescue from this awful roadside attraction down south—and his teeth are completely shot. So I have to use this heavy-duty commercial grinder for his meals to get the consistency right. If the texture isn't perfect, he just spits it out on the dirt and glares at you. He's got these massive, intense yellow eyes. It's actually kind of funny, he acts more like a spoiled house cat than a mountain lion sometimes. I had to take the whole meat grinder apart last week because a bone fragment jammed the auger, and my hands were just covered in grease for days... 

Um, wait. Sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling out of control. But yeah, during the eating, I definitely want to stop. I just can't.
Do these eating episodes cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life, like your work, relationships, or how you see yourself?

Yeah, it really does... it messes with my head a lot. It's definitely affecting how I see myself, and it's starting to bleed into my work, too. Like, last week, we had this big bilingual outreach presentation for some local schools. I'm usually the one who handles the Spanish-speaking groups because my mom's family is from Colombia, so I grew up speaking it. My abuela actually used to make these amazing arepas, like, perfectly crispy on the outside but soft inside, and she'd serve them with this slow-roasted pork... 

Anyway, the presentation. We were doing this whole talk about conservation efforts for the jaguars, and usually I love doing it. Jaguars are incredible swimmers, by the way, which most people don't know. They actually hunt caimans in the rivers. But during the presentation, I was just... I was so distracted. All I could think about was getting out of there, going home, and just starting the whole eating cycle again. I was so in my own head about it that I completely stumbled through parts of the talk. I kept losing my place, and I'm pretty sure my coworkers noticed something was off. It was embarrassing. So, yeah, it's definitely causing me a lot of distress.
After these eating episodes, do you ever try to compensate for the food you’ve eaten, like by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising a lot?

Yeah, I... I do. After I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up. It just feels like the only way to undo it, you know? Like I have to get it out before the calories settle in and become permanent. 

It's actually awful because the plumbing in my apartment building is so old. The pipes make this horrendous groaning noise every time you flush. The super, Gary, he's this older guy who's always wearing these faded mechanic shirts... he says the pipes were installed back in the 60s and the whole system needs to be replaced. But the landlord is too cheap to do it. Gary's actually a pretty cool guy, though. He helped me fix my truck last month. It's a '98 Tacoma, and I use it to haul feed sometimes when the zoo's main delivery truck breaks down. The suspension is totally shot, though. Every time I hit a pothole on I-95, it feels like the whole chassis is going to rattle apart. I really need to get the shocks replaced, but it's just so expensive, and... 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? But yeah, the throwing up. That's... that's what I do.
How often do you experience these episodes of feeling out of control while eating followed by making yourself vomit?

It's usually at least one night a week. Always when I'm alone at my place. I'd say it's been happening at this frequency for... probably at least the last four months. 

Actually, four months ago is exactly when we had to move all the reptiles into their winter enclosures at the zoo. We have this Aldabra giant tortoise named Tank, and moving him is a literal nightmare. He weighs like five hundred pounds, and if he decides he doesn't want to walk, he just drops his shell to the dirt and turns into a boulder. It took four of us and a whole bucket of papayas to finally coax him into the transport crate. Papayas are his absolute favorite, and he gets the juice all over his beak. It's kind of cute but incredibly messy. My uniform smelled like fermented fruit for a week because our industrial washer in the breakroom broke down. They had to order a replacement motor from Germany, which took forever because it got held up in customs, and... 

Man, I'm sorry. I'm rambling again. My brain just completely drifts off. But yeah, to answer your question, for the past four months, it's been at least once a week. I'll be by myself at night, end up eating way, way more than I ever meant to, and then I'll go make myself throw it up.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (self-induced vomiting) at least once a week for the past four months. This meets the frequency criterion for bulimia nervosa. There is no indication of anorexia nervosa (F50.0) as the patient does not describe restrictive eating or fear of weight gain in the context of significantly low weight.

F50.0 (Anorexia nervosa) remains as a candidate due to the patient's focus on controlling food intake and body image concerns, but is less prominent. No other disorders were ruled out at this time.
